Xash3D-FWGS-XBOX · frame-time recorder · original Xbox hardware

Real console, v0.1.3: c2a2 (long session)

A 151-minute session on a retail Xbox with the v0.1.3 build, spent in c2a2, c2a2a, c2a2b1 and c2a2b2: no frame over 250 ms.

Frame rate over the session

Hover or tap the chart for a reading.
fps, each second of play 60 fps (16.7 ms) 30 fps (33.3 ms) level load

Where each frame's time went

CPU (engine work) GPU wait (CPU blocked on the GPU) vblank / swap wait between frames (frame limiter) 16.7 ms 33.3 ms

Work per frame over the session

draws vertices pushbuffer dwords each line is a per-second mean over frames in play, scaled to its own session peak (the readout gives the values)

Per map

In-play frames only (not loading, no menu or pause), leaving out a map's first 30 frames. Min and max fps are the slowest and fastest one-second windows. 1% low is the frame rate the slowest 1% of frames fall below (1000 / the 99th-percentile frame time). CPU and GPU are milliseconds per frame. Free memory is sampled at the last flush before the load and at the first frame of the map. Frames that wrote the recording to the disk (every 5 s and at each map start; their time includes the write) are left out of the statistics (--include-flush keeps them): 301 in this file, the Flushes column gives their mean / worst ms. Click a row to mark it on the charts.

MapPlayedAvg fpsMinMax1% lowWorst msCPU msGPU msGPU-bound>16.7 ms>33.3 msSplitFlushesLoad sMiB free before / at start

CPU by subsystem

Milliseconds per in-play frame, the same frames as the per-map table. Each span is the time inside one call (SV_Physics, SCR_UpdateScreen, the client's StudioDrawModel...) minus the renderer's GPU/vblank/swap waits inside it, so it is CPU work. Spans nest, shown by indentation: incl includes the spans under it, own is what is left without them, % is incl as a share of the frame's CPU. The top-level spans cover every call Host_Frame makes; unattributed is CPU that no span saw. Where each span is measured: docs/r3d/frametime-recorder.md.

Level changes and stalls

A level-change frame is the frame whose Host_Frame queued a changelevel or a load: it still starts in play, but the engine runs the load before the next Host_Frame, so the load is this frame's time between host frames. 7 in this file, left out of the per-map statistics (--include-level-change keeps them). Found by the recorder's LOAD flag, or in a file recorded before it existed by their shape: one of the last 2 in-play frames before a load, with at least 100 ms between host frames.

sMap → nextTotal msCPU msBetween msFound by

Stalls: in-play frames over 250 ms

Level-change frames left out. A stall that is mostly CPU happened inside Host_Frame (an autosave, a synchronous read); frames that wrote the recording are marked.

None.

Work per frame

What the renderer submitted in each in-play frame, counted where ref/nv2a submits it: mean / peak per map. These are counts, not times, so they are the same in xemu as on the console — an xemu run measures them exactly. Draws are draw submissions (a world run, a 2D/TriAPI batch, a decal); prims the BEGIN/END blocks they split into; PB KiB the pushbuffer written in the frame; verts every vertex or index submitted (world, studio, TriAPI, 2D, decals); LM texels the lightmap texels rebuilt on the CPU.

What the frame time follows

Over every in-play frame of the session: each counter's mean and peak, and Pearson's r against the frame's CPU time and its GPU wait. A strong r says the time rises and falls with that work.

GPU-bound frames against the rest

Per map, the mean work of frames with more than 1 ms of GPU wait next to the frames without: work that is much higher in the first column is what made the CPU wait for the GPU.

The 10 frames with the most GPU wait

CPU and GPU

Each frame is timed with the Pentium III's time-stamp counter, calibrated against the kernel's performance counter (733.33 MHz in this file). CPU is the engine's own work: Host_Frame minus the renderer's waits. GPU wait is the time the CPU spun on pb_busy() because the GPU still had work queued. The NV2A runs in parallel with the CPU and pbkit exposes no GPU-side timestamp, so this is the GPU's excess over the CPU, not its busy time: near zero means the GPU kept up and the frame was CPU-bound; a large value means the GPU held the frame. GPU-bound counts frames with more than 1 ms of GPU wait.

Waits and the rest

vblank / swap is time in pb_wait_for_vbl() and in pb_finished() while all three back buffers were queued for display. Between frames is the time outside Host_Frame: the engine's frame limiter (fps_max) and the platform loop. A frame's total is start to next start, so the timeline is wall-clock time.

Work counters
